goldens.comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/features/apps/components/CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx:39 — Successful cache deletion never invalidates connectedCalendars, leaving the destructive-action status stale in the UI.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, in CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx, the deleteCacheMutation (lines 39-47) only calls onSuccess?.() on success, but does NOT invalidate connectedCalendars. In contrast, the disconnectMutation (lines 49-62) properly invalidates both connectedCalendars and integrations in onSettled. Since the connectedCalendars query returns cacheUpdatedAt (as shown in connectedCalendars.handler.ts enrichment), after deleting the cache, the UI would still show the old cacheUpdatedAt value until a manual refresh. This is a real bug - the cache status in the dropdown would be stale after deletion.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/features/apps/components/CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx:43 — Deleting cache never invalidates connectedCalendars, so its cache status/action remains visible from stale query data.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the deleteCacheMutation in CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx (lines 43-51) only calls onSuccess callback but does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query. In contrast, the disconnectMutation (lines 53-66) properly invalidates both connectedCalendars and integrations queries in its onSettled handler. Since the cache status (cacheUpdatedAt) is fetched via the connectedCalendars query (as shown in connectedCalendars.handler.ts which enriches results with cacheStatusMap), after deleting the cache, the UI will still show stale cache status data until the user manually refreshes or navigates away. This is a real bug where the cache deletion succeeds but the UI doesn't reflect the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:1024 — Updating SelectedCalendar.updatedAt is dead parallel cache state because cache status is sourced from CalendarCache.updatedAt.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that updating SelectedCalendar.updatedAt is 'dead parallel cache state' because cache status comes from CalendarCache.updatedAt. However, looking at the diff, the code in CalendarService.ts calls `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` with an empty data object `{}`. This appears to be intentionally triggering the `updatedAt` auto-update on SelectedCalendar records (Prisma's @updatedAt behavior). The SelectedCalendar.updatedAt field is used elsewhere in the codebase (as shown in getConnectedDestinationCalendars.ts where updatedAt is now included in the select). The cache status displayed in the UI does come from CalendarCache via getCacheStatusByCredentialIds, but the SelectedCalendar.updatedAt serves a different purpose - tracking when calendars were last synced/updated. These are not redundant parallel states but serve different purposes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/features/calendar-cache/calendar-cache.repository.ts:173 — Cache-status lookup aggregates every cache row for each credential on every connected-calendars request because no [credentialId, updatedAt] index supports the maximum timestamp.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` method that uses `prisma.calendarCache.groupBy` with `_max: { updatedAt: true }` on the `credentialId` field. This query aggregates across all CalendarCache rows for the given credentials. The finding correctly identifies that without an index on [credentialId, updatedAt], this aggregation could be slow at scale. However, this is a performance concern rather than a bug - the code will function correctly. The schema.prisma changes show CalendarCache has a credentialId field but no compound index with updatedAt is visible. This is a valid architectural/performance concern for the new functionality.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:1024 — A post-refresh timestamp write can reject after cache and unwatch side effects succeed, causing callers to retry an already-completed operation.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that line 1024 adds a call to `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` at the end of a method. Looking at the context, this is inside what appears to be a method that fetches availability and sets cache. The finding claims this 'post-refresh timestamp write can reject after cache and unwatch side effects succeed', but the diff doesn't show any 'unwatch side effects' in this method - it only shows cache operations and then this new update call. The finding appears to be speculating about error handling scenarios that aren't clearly demonstrated by the diff. The method structure shown doesn't indicate complex side effects that would be problematic if this final call fails. The finding mischaracterizes what the code does.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/calendars/deleteCache.handler.ts:14 — The new cache-status and cache-deletion behavior has no automated tests covering ownership, empty cache, or UI mutation outcomes.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces new functionality: a deleteCache handler (deleteCache.handler.ts), cache status retrieval (getCacheStatusByCredentialIds), and UI components (CredentialActionsDropdown.tsx) for managing calendar cache. This is non-trivial business logic involving ownership verification, database mutations, and UI state management. The finding correctly identifies that no test files are included in this diff for this new functionality. While 'add more tests' generically would be too vague, this finding specifically identifies the new cache-related features that lack test coverage, which is a legitimate review concern for newly added nontrivial logic.
